newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain, China have long way to go on HK issues.
newsitem.headline: Britain, China have long way to go on HK issues.

text.p: Despite some progress in recent weeks, Chinese and British teams hammering out details of Hong Kong's handover on July 1 still have many crucial issues to address at meetings in London this week.
"We are re-doubling our efforts in the hope that we can complete most of the outstanding work at the next JLG (Joint Liaison Group) meeting," Hong Kong's Chief Secretary Anson Chan said last week.
"But we need cooperation from both sides and are acutely aware that time is running out."
The JLG is the Sino-British diplomatic body handling the territory's return to China at midnight on June 30.

The process of sorting through the transfer of sovereignty over the wealthy territory of 6.4 million people has inched along since London and Beijing signed an accord on the handover in 1984, and outright agreement has often proved elusive.
Deadlocks over citizenship rights, reciprocal enforcement of laws and the handover ceremony have all slowed the negotiations.
But there have also been positive signals.

China's senior representative Zhao Jihua told reporters on Friday he was optimistic the London meetings could resolve issues such as the definition of permanent residency, the posting of People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops in Hong Kong before July 1 and arrangements for the handover ceremony.
But the Chinese side may just wait out the British on some of the other issues, Michael DeGolyer of Hong Kong Baptist University told Reuters on Sunday.

"The Chinese tradition or custom is usually to wait till the last minute and then about 10 ticks past before coming to agreement," he said. "On some of these things, I think the Chinese side has just decided that they're going to do what they're going to do regardless of what the British side says."
Despite the deadlocks, some of the arrangements are already going ahead.
On Saturday, the Hong Kong government began inviting foreign media to cover the handover events after getting the go-ahead from the JLG on March 5.

But the list of dignitaries and other guests who will attend the 4,000-seat banquet and ceremony marking the change of sovereignty is as incomplete as the HK$4.8 billion (US$620 million) extension to the Convention Centre hurriedly being completed to house the gala event on the night of June 30.
Working out who to include has become a thorny issue for the JLG negotiators, particularly on representatives from Taiwan, which China regards as a renegade province.

DeGolyer said the JLG has been focusing on "the trivia" of the arrangements or on the larger sovereignty questions, but it is uncertainty over "daily life" issues -- right of abode, work visas, extradition of criminals and the like -- that is causing "anxiety and confusion" among Hong Kong people.
"I don't think China has thought this one through very well," DeGolyer said, adding that the Chinese had not fully realised the intricacies of applying the law in a post-British Hong Kong.
"They can't quite grasp why on earth you'd have to go through all this," he said.

China has promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy under the "one country, two systems" policy devised by late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping and laid out in the Basic Law, the territory's post-handover constitution.
But Beijing has raised fears by proposing to repeal some Hong Kong legislation enshrining civil rights -- ordinances it says are not consistent with the Basic Law.
